Inflation in pictures: what your future budget needs to buy

Use charts and editable scenarios to explore future living costs, the purchasing power of unchanged cash and the difference between nominal and real returns.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

A future dollar amount needs a price-level assumption. Compare what the money can buy as well as the number printed on the account statement.

01

Start with the cost of a familiar budget

The first chart grows today’s monthly cost at the selected annual inflation rate. It holds the quantity and quality of the spending basket constant. If your family, housing or lifestyle changes, that is a separate planning adjustment rather than an inflation effect.

A monthly budget of CAD 3,000 at a constant 3% inflation assumption becomes about CAD 6,281 after 25 years. This is an original calculation, not a forecast of Canadian prices. The increase compounds: applying 3% to the original budget every year without increasing the base would understate it.

The Bank of Canada’s inflation overview describes CPI and its inflation-target framework. A policy target is not a promise that prices or your personal expenses will grow at that rate every year. Use more than one assumption for a long horizon.

02

See the difference between stable dollars and stable purchasing power

The second chart holds a cash amount at CAD 10,000 with no nominal interest. Its purchasing power is shown in today’s dollars after fixed comparison periods. The nominal balance remains unchanged, while positive inflation reduces the goods and services it can purchase.

This is not an argument that every dollar should be invested in risky assets. Money needed for an imminent bill has a different role from long-term retirement capital. Liquidity and the ability to make a payment on time can justify holding cash even when its real return is low.

Compare the emergency-fund guide for that distinction. An emergency reserve is designed to absorb a cash-flow shock. A growth portfolio is exposed to market risk and may be down precisely when the money is needed.

03

Translate nominal return into a real return

The matrix compares assumed nominal returns with inflation rates. A positive account return can still mean a loss of purchasing power. The exact relationship is real return = (1 + nominal return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.

For example, a 5% nominal return with 3% inflation gives a real return of about 1.94%, before tax and fees. Subtracting 3% from 5% is a useful approximation at modest rates, but it is not the exact compounding relationship.

These cells are sensitivity calculations, not estimates of investment success. The matrix does not assign probabilities, and it does not allow you to choose a return simply because it is needed to meet a goal.

04

Your spending basket can differ from the average

A household that rents, a household with a fixed mortgage payment, and a household facing large care expenses may experience different pressures. An aggregate price index is useful context but cannot reconstruct every household’s cost changes.

Build your own starting basket from actual recurring spending. Separate price changes from changes in quantity, such as moving to a larger home or adding a family member. For a detailed plan, examine major categories separately rather than hiding every uncertainty in one average rate.

Do not combine a real return with a second inflation deduction. If both future cash flows and portfolio returns are expressed in today’s dollars, maintain that basis throughout the model. If the model is nominal, inflate the expenses and use nominal returns consistently.

05

Put an inflation review into the plan

  1. Write the goal in today’s dollars and retain that baseline.
  2. Test at least a lower and higher inflation assumption.
  3. Identify expenses whose prices or quantities could change differently.
  4. Check whether income sources adjust with prices, and under what terms.
  5. Update the budget from observed spending rather than only changing the forecast rate.

A spending plan becomes easier to review when nominal amounts, real amounts, dates and assumptions are clearly labelled. The charts are designed to make those relationships visible before a more detailed tax, benefit or investment model is added.
